items.caption:
Microsoft has been working on Project Silica for nearly a decade, and this month marked its biggest leap yet.

The research phase is now officially complete, and the system no longer requires rare, expensive glass. 

It now works with the same heat-resistant material found in Pyrex cookware. That solves what was previously the biggest barrier to real-world deployment. 

The glass stores nearly 5 terabytes of data in a coaster-sized slab, needs no power to maintain it, and is immune to heat, water, and magnetic fields that would destroy conventional storage within decades.

Microsoft has already used it to archive the 1978 Superman film and partnered with the Global Music Vault to preserve recordings under Arctic ice.

You can read more about it in their latest research paper, details below👇

Study: “Laser writing in glass for dense, fast and efficient archival data storage” published in Nature
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-025-10042-w
items.transcript: Microsoft just etched nearly 5 terabytes of data into a piece of glass the size of a coaster, and it's supposed to survive for 10,000 years. This is Project Silica, a storage system that uses ultra-fast lasers to write data directly into glass. Each laser pulse lasts one trillionth of a second and carves microscopic structures called voxels into 301 layers inside ordinary glass, the same kind that your food storage container is probably made out of. To read the data, a microscope captures images of each layer and an image recognition model decodes the patterns with zero errors. The glass needs no power to maintain its data. It's immune to heat, water, radiation, and magnetic fields that would normally wipe conventional hard drives over the years. Accelerated aging tests predict the data will survive past 10,000 years at room temperature, twice as long as the oldest known writing in the world. Today's cloud archives consume enormous amounts of energy just keeping the data alive on degrading magnetic tape. but glass storage needs none of that. Microsoft is targeting cloud providers, national archives, and media companies as potential customers for this. The write speeds are still slower than conventional storage, but for data to last thousands of years, the trade-off might be worth it. items.caption:
🦂 Claude just helped design a potential scorpion antivenom. 

In 64 hours, an internal research model generated over 318,000 protein designs, guided by five human messages. 

Anthropic’s scientists and Citrini Research sent 211 designs to outside labs for testing and 17 met the study’s binding criteria. 

These tiny proteins grab scorpion toxins, potentially blocking their attack on nerve cells. 

But binding isn’t the same as neutralizing venom…

The team hasn’t tested whether they protect cells or animals, and each successful design bound only one toxin. 

It’s an early research result with a much bigger question ahead. Can these molecules eventually become safe and effective medicines?

Research paper: “De novo design of protein binders against scorpion toxins with Claude”
items.transcript: So in case you missed it, CLOG just helped design a potential scorpion antivenom. In 64 hours, it generated 318,000 protein designs guided by just five human messages. Outside labs then tested 211 of those designs and 17 passed the study's binding tests. For context, these are tiny proteins designed to grab the part of a toxin that attacks your nerves. See, scorpion neurotoxins interfere with sodium channels, the molecular gates that help nerve cells fire. And that disruption can trigger a dangerous surge of stress chemicals and, in severe cases, heart failure. The idea is to cover the toxins' docking site before it can reach those channels. The project actually brought together investment researchers from Citrini and anthropic scientists using an internal version of Claude and specialized design tools. But we still don't know whether grabbing these toxins actually stops them. See it's still really early and nobody has actually tested it in cells or animals yet. Each successful protein only bound one toxin, so they're still far away from the universal antivenom. But still, these designs made it out of a computer and into a lab, where scientists confirmed they could grab their targets. But the next challenge is actually finding out whether any of them can help someone who's been stung in the real world. items.caption:
🧠 An AI system called Brain-IT can reconstruct recognizable images from brain scans of people looking at pictures.

Developed at the Weizmann Institute, it predicts both image content and layout, then uses a diffusion model to generate the reconstruction. 

Researchers expanded its training data with simulated brain activity. With one hour of scans from a new person, it achieved results comparable to earlier systems trained on 40 hours. 

But it still makes mistakes: one reconstruction turned a dog into a goat. 

Reconstructing dreams is a future ambition. For now, the system reconstructs viewed pictures, with impressive results that remain imperfect predictions.

Study: “Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer”

DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2510.25976
items.transcript: This AI can turn a brain scan into a picture of what you're looking at. It can reconstruct both the objects you saw and how they were arranged. Researchers developed an AI system called Brain IT that analyzes fMRI scans which track changes in blood oxygenation associated with brain activity. Basically, one branch predicts the image's layout and colors, and another predicts its content, like a bunch of bananas on a plate. And then those clues guide a diffusion model to generate a reconstruction. But there was a problem with this because collecting brain scans is very expensive, so the team trained another model to work backwards. It takes an ordinary image and predicts the brain activity someone might produce while looking at it. And those simulated recordings provide extra training examples without putting anyone inside a scanner. And with just one hour of scans from one new person, the researchers reported results comparable to earlier systems trained on 40 hours. But these images are still predictions. In one example, a dog in a bathtub became a goat. But it's very fascinating because the researchers hope to eventually reconstruct entire dreams. But for now, they've still demonstrated something very remarkable, turning brain activity into recognizable versions of pictures people actually saw. 🥊 This robot cage fight just got hit with a cease-and-desist letter.

@frankielap faced three humanoid robots, getting knocked down repeatedly and injuring his hand despite wearing boxing gloves.

Human pilots controlled each robot remotely through VR, throwing punches without stepping into the cage.

California’s athletic commission says the event needed its approval. 

The company argues the law defines a match as a contest between two people.

So if someone fights you through a robot, does that count as two people fighting?
items.transcript: So we need to talk about the robot cage fighting that's happening in San Francisco right now. California's athletic mission just sent the organizers a cease and desist letter. This honestly feels like a news story straight out of a sci-fi movie. See, this startup called Robot Entertainment Combat put this guy, Frankie, an influencer you've probably seen on the internet, in a cage with a six foot steel framed humanoid. But to be clear, there was another human behind the machine. A pilot was controlling the robot remotely through a VR system. So Frankie was basically fighting someone who could throw punches without physically being inside the cage. Inside the cage, he faced three different robots getting repeatedly knocked down. And even with boxing gloves on, he injured his hand punching one of their metal frames. California's Athletic Commission says combat exhibitions involving a human require its approval, but the company argues that the law defines a match as a contest between two people, which leaves a new strange question up for debate. If a human controls the punches, but a machine delivers them, who exactly is fighting? If you want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI and robotics, Follow for more.

🐄 Halter, a New Zealand agtech startup, has developed AI-powered smart collars that create virtual fences for cattle, allowing farmers to manage herds remotely through a phone app.

The collars use sound and vibration cues to guide cows, collect over 6,000 data points per minute, and use machine learning to track grazing, predict disease, and detect breeding cycles.

Founded by Craig Piggott, who grew up on a dairy farm, Halter now manages nearly 650,000 cows across 1,300 farms in New Zealand, Australia, and the United States.

The company recently raised $220 million at a $2 billion valuation 👀
items.transcript: This cow collar is replacing thousands of miles of cattle fencing using what they call the cow algorithm. And it just turned this New Zealand startup into a billion dollar company. Halter makes AI powered smart collars that create virtual fences for cattle.
